assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock is a measurement instrument in the strict sense: the magic-wavelength idea turned many neutral atoms into a clock with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, which in turn enables relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches. Original, clearly defined, and with a clear route to uses beyond atomic physics. It builds on the frequency-comb and ion-clock work already honored, but the lattice clock itself is distinct.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first demonstrations. Ye's group carried the strontium clock to the 1e-18 regime, with the comb link and the many-body and cavity-based clock work. Two laureates is a clean and fair configuration. Other contributors (e.g. Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom in Ye's group, and the Paris/PTB/NIST groups) exist but the decisive credit is reasonably clear.
assessment.maturity: Several independent labs have reproduced the performance, clock comparisons exist across continents, and the 2019 redefinition roadmap for the second keeps the clocks in the discussion. Mature and timely, with a long record of reproducibility.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would wish to include a third contributor for the ytterbium clocks or the ion-clock lineage is not settled by the supplied credit.
I recall, without having verified it here, that Katori's idea had earlier theoretical precursors; the exact priority split is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gave inertial sensors of extraordinary sensitivity: gravimeters, gyroscopes, measurement of G and the fine-structure constant, tests of the equivalence principle. It is a case where a new measurement method opened new ways of observing nature, and the field now supports quantum-sensing technology. Conceptually and experimentally important.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard established atom interferometry with gratings and material optics, Bordé provided the theoretical framework and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, and Kasevich made the precision light-pulse inertial sensors. This matches the three-person structure well. Chu and Chapman, among others, also contributed, and Chu has a Nobel Prize for another discovery already, which complicates a fair configuration.
assessment.maturity: Mature after three decades, with commercial gravimeters and independent groups worldwide. Large-scale space and long-baseline tests are still in progress, but the core achievement is secure.
uncertainties: Credit for light-pulse interferometry is shared among more people than three; omission of Steven Chu and others is a risk.
The strongest fundamental-physics results are still being refined, so impact beyond metrology is partly prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Controlled coupling between single photons and atoms or ensembles, with cavity QED, EIT-based storage and heralded entanglement, underpins quantum memories and networks. This is close to my own field and I appreciate that the experimental demonstrations (storage of light, atom-photon state transfer, single-atom photon sources, memory-enhanced links) were hard and decisive. Important and original, though the label is broad.
assessment.attribution: Kimble's quantum-network and cavity-QED program, Rempe's single-atom cavity work and photon-pistol and state-transfer experiments, and Lukin's EIT-based storage and later network work form a coherent set. Credit also properly extends to Hau (slow light), Polzik, Gisin, Kuzmich, Lvovsky and the rare-earth-crystal groups, so a three-person selection involves real judgments.
assessment.maturity: Still developing: long-distance quantum repeaters and fault-tolerant networks are not yet realized, though the elementary building blocks have been reproduced by many groups.
uncertainties: The candidate is a compound of several platforms (atoms, ensembles, solid-state memories) that may not fit under one prize citation.
As a member whose own research is in rare-earth quantum memories, I should be cautious about my assessment of the relative merit of this area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller's proposal for a quantum computer with trapped ions and their later proposals for quantum simulation with cold atoms and Rydberg gates set the agenda for experimental AMO quantum information. The theory is clear, original and has had very large impact on experiment. I would weigh it against actual experimental demonstration, which came from others.
assessment.attribution: Two laureates is a natural configuration, since the two share the central trapped-ion gate proposal and the Jaksch-Zoller cold-atom proposals. The question is whether the prize should be for theory when the experimental recipients (Wineland and Haroche) were already honored in 2012.
assessment.maturity: Proposal made in 1995 and widely validated by experiments in ions, atoms and other platforms. Mature and timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with candidates on optical-lattice quantum simulation and neutral-atom arrays may split the recognition.
Wineland's 2012 prize may be seen as having covered part of the ion-trap quantum-computing recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV centers in diamond brought room-temperature single-spin readout and led to nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and bio-sensing. It is a striking measurement-oriented advance with applications reaching into biology and materials science. Original and widely used.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's single-NV optical detection in 1997 is the founding experimental step. Lukin and Walsworth made the sensing demonstrations with Harvard. Credit is also due to Awschalom, Hanson, Jelezko, Taylor, Yacoby and others, so any three-person choice leaves out significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: The sensing results are replicated by many groups and commercial instruments exist, but some application claims (e.g. in vivo and single-molecule NMR) are still maturing.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested and diffuse; Jelezko, Hanson, Awschalom and Yacoby are plausible alternates.
Sensitivity limits and benefits over competing methods are still being established for some applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping and cooling of antiprotons and antihydrogen and the precision comparison of matter and antimatter (g-2 of the electron and positron, CPT tests, 1S-2S and hyperfine spectroscopy, the antihydrogen gravity measurement) are impressive experimental accomplishments. The core question, the tests of CPT and fundamental symmetries, is clear and well motivated.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse led the single-particle Penning trap measurements and antihydrogen with ATRAP; Hangst led the ALPHA trapping and spectroscopy. Other significant credit exists for the ATHENA and ASACUSA collaborations (Amoretti, Doser, Yamazaki, Hori), so fairness to collaborations is an issue.
assessment.maturity: Measurements are progressing and reproducible, though precision is still well below that of ordinary hydrogen, and no violation has been seen. Some may argue that impact is still a promise.
uncertainties: Whether the prize is for the trapping technology or the measurements is unclear.
Competing collaborations (ALPHA, ATRAP, ASACUSA, AEgIS) complicate attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light has been demonstrated to beat the standard quantum limit in practice and is now installed in gravitational-wave detectors, so a quantum-optics idea has measurable consequences for astronomy. As an experimentalist who thinks in terms of noise floors, I value this very much. It is a clear case of a new measurement capability.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the theory of squeezed-light interferometry; Kimble's group (Wu et al., 1986) and Slusher et al. demonstrated squeezing; Schnabel, Mavalvala and others brought it into GEO600 and LIGO. Slusher and Walls, and others, are missing from the credited names, so the configuration is unsatisfactory without a decision on the experimental pioneers.
assessment.maturity: Operationally mature: it has been used routinely in detectors since about 2011 (GEO600) and 2019 (LIGO/Virgo). Gain in the sensitivity of observations is well documented.
uncertainties: Partial overlap with the 2017 gravitational-wave prize may reduce enthusiasm.
The priority among early squeezing experimenters is not fully clear to me from memory, and Kimble also appears under a different candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, with the Mott insulator transition and quantum gas microscopes, gives access to many-body physics at the level of single sites and spins. Important and now a major field, offering controlled measurement of strongly correlated matter. It builds on the BEC and optical-lattice prizes.
assessment.attribution: Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition (with Hänsch), Esslinger did the fermionic work and the Fermi-Hubbard realizations, and Bloch and Greiner developed gas microscopes. Cirac and Zoller are credited in the proposal but are listed under a separate candidate; the credit allocation across them is awkward.
assessment.maturity: Methods are reproduced by many groups; however, convincing quantum advantage for open problems such as the Hubbard model phase diagram is still in progress.
uncertainties: Overlap with the Cirac-Zoller candidate means that two ballots may point to partly the same achievement.
Jaksch, Hänsch and Kasevich (2001) group contributions in the early optical-lattice work are not accounted for in the supplied names.
